931.event_title: Francois Blanc turns big wins into bait at the Monte Carlo casino
931.event: Facing bankruptcy, Prince Charles III of Monaco in 1863 gave the casino concession to Francois Blanc, who had already run a successful casino at Bad Homburg. Since every casino game is weighted in favour of the house, most players lost in the long run, but Blanc made a public ceremony of any player who broke the bank, covering the table with a black cloth while fresh money was fetched, because he knew that news of a big win drew in crowds of new gamblers hoping to repeat it. The casino soon made Monaco rich, and the principality's own residents have ever since been forbidden to gamble in its casinos.
931.explanation: The business of Monte Carlo rested on the fact that a well-publicised win costs the house little and lures many more people into losing.
931.tie_back: The kural says not to desire gambling even when you can win, because the winnings are like the bait a fish swallows with the hook inside, and Blanc deliberately used other people's winnings as bait.
931._accuracy_note: The casino's own method makes the bait-and-hook image almost literal; the kural addresses the individual gambler, while the event shows the house's side.

932.event_title: Lord Holland agrees to pay the gambling debts of his son Charles James Fox
932.event: Charles James Fox, the brilliant young member of Parliament and later Britain's first foreign secretary, became notorious in his early twenties for reckless gambling, which caused his parents great unhappiness; within a month of reaching Oxford he had written to his father that he hoped never to play again but could not promise it. In November 1773 his father, Lord Holland, agreed to pay his son's debts up to one hundred thousand pounds, and an Eton College account records that on one occasion his father paid debts of 140,000 pounds. Even after a year in which he won enormously, Fox was soon in debt again, and in 1781 bailiffs were in his house while he was running a faro bank at Brooks's club.
932.explanation: Fox's occasional large wins never changed the overall result: his gambling consumed sums his family and friends repeatedly had to make good.
932.tie_back: The kural says gamblers gain one and lose a hundred, and Fox's winning seasons were swallowed by losses so large that his father had to pay debts of over a hundred thousand pounds.
932._accuracy_note: The sources differ on the exact sum paid, so the figures are given as each source states them; Fox's political greatness shows that the kural's claim about no good path of life is not literally borne out.

933.event_title: The Louisiana Lottery drains money from across the United States until Congress closes the mails to it
933.event: The Louisiana State Lottery Company, a private corporation chartered in 1868, sold tickets in almost every state, drawing about 90 percent of its sales from outside Louisiana and paying its stockholders dividends of well over 100 percent a year between 1887 and 1890. Other states, unhappy that their citizens' money was flowing to the company, pressed President Benjamin Harrison to act, and in September 1890 he signed a law banning lottery tickets and advertisements from the mail; the Postmaster General soon reported that business at the company's New Orleans office had fallen off by a third. Louisiana refused to renew the company's charter, which expired at the end of 1893.
933.explanation: Millions of small stakes from players across the country became extraordinary profits for a handful of shareholders, which is why so many states fought to shut the lottery down.
933.tie_back: The kural says that the wealth of one who keeps calling stakes on the rolling dice leaves him and falls into the hands of others, and the Louisiana Lottery's ticket buyers steadily enriched its owners.
933._accuracy_note: Shows wealth passing from many gamblers into other hands, but through a lottery rather than the dice the kural names, and at the level of a whole country rather than one gambler.

934.event_title: Beau Brummell flees England to escape his gambling debts
934.place: London, England, and Calais and Caen, France
934.event: George Bryan Brummell, the leader of London fashion and friend of the Prince Regent, inherited a fortune of about 30,000 pounds in 1799, but gambling and extravagance exhausted it, and on 16 May 1816 he fled to Calais to escape his creditors. He spent the rest of his life in France, hopelessly in debt, was imprisoned for debt in Caen in 1835, and after two strokes was given shelter in the charitable asylum of Bon Sauveur in Caen. He died there in 1840, a pauper.
934.explanation: The most admired man in Regency society ended his life poor, dishonoured and forgotten abroad.
934.tie_back: The kural says nothing brings poverty like gambling, which causes many miseries and destroys a person's good name, and gambling took both Brummell's fortune and his place in society.
934._accuracy_note: A clear case of gambling leading to poverty and the loss of standing; extravagance as well as gambling contributed to his ruin.

935.event_title: Charles Wells, the man who broke the bank at Monte Carlo, ends in prison
935.place: Monte Carlo, Monaco, and London, England
935.event: In 1891 the Englishman Charles Deville Wells, who had arrived at Monte Carlo with only a few hundred pounds, played roulette every day from opening to closing and broke the bank several times, winning tens of thousands of pounds; he said he had a system, and a popular song made him famous. On a third visit in January 1892 his luck turned, he lost heavily, and he cabled his backers for more money, which he also lost, until he was so short of cash that he was selling coal from his yacht. Arrested at Le Havre, he was convicted in London on 14 March 1893 of obtaining money by false pretences from investors in his worthless inventions, and sentenced to eight years' penal servitude.
935.explanation: The most celebrated winner of his age was soon left with nothing, and the money he had staked turned out to have been taken from others.
935.tie_back: The kural speaks of those who prided themselves on the dice, the gaming hall and their own skill and ended up with nothing, and Wells, who claimed a winning system and lived at the tables, finished bankrupt and in prison.
935._accuracy_note: Very close to the kural's picture of the proud, skilful gambler brought to nothing; his ruin also involved fraud, not gambling alone.

936.event_title: Girolamo Cardano's gambling sends his family to the poorhouse
936.place: Gallarate and Milan, Duchy of Milan (now Italy)
936.event: The physician and mathematician Girolamo Cardano, later famous for the Ars Magna, had squandered his father's small bequest and turned to cards, dice and chess to make a living. In 1533, unable to practise medicine after the Milan College of Physicians refused him, he went back to gambling, and things went so badly that he had to pawn his wife's jewellery and some of their furniture. When the family moved to Milan they fared even worse and had to enter the poorhouse; his biographers note that gambling remained an addiction for many years that cost him time, money and reputation.
936.explanation: One of the finest minds of the Renaissance, who even wrote the first mathematical study of games of chance, could not keep his family fed while gambling held him.
936.tie_back: The kural says those swallowed by the misfortune called gambling will never have their bellies filled and will suffer many sorrows, and Cardano's gambling brought his household to the poorhouse.
936._accuracy_note: Poverty and sorrow from gambling are well documented; Cardano later recovered and prospered, which the kural's never does not allow for.

937.event_title: Young Leo Tolstoy's gambling debts cost him the house where he was born
937.event: Leo Tolstoy inherited the family estate of Yasnaya Polyana in 1847, but as a young man he gambled heavily, and by the time he married in 1862 he had sold half his land and the estate's main house to pay gambling debts. The large manor house in which he had been born was sold in 1854 while he was away in the army, taken apart and carried off to the village of Dolgoye, about 40 kilometres away, where it stood until it was demolished in 1913. Tolstoy lived the rest of his life in one of the two smaller wings, and a stone marks the spot where the house once stood.
937.explanation: The ancestral home built by his grandfather and father was lost to the card tables before Tolstoy had written his great novels.
937.tie_back: The kural says that time spent in the gaming hall destroys a person's inherited wealth, and Tolstoy's gambling literally carried off the family house he had inherited.
937._accuracy_note: A near-literal case of inherited wealth lost to gambling; the museum's own history records the sale without naming the cause, which comes from the scholarly source, and Tolstoy later rebuilt the family fortune and reformed his character.

938.event_title: Pete Rose is banned from baseball and denies betting on the game for years
938.place: New York and Cincinnati, United States
938.event: After a six-month investigation found that Pete Rose, baseball's all-time hits leader and manager of the Cincinnati Reds, had bet on baseball games including those of his own team between 1985 and 1987, Commissioner Bart Giamatti placed him on the permanently ineligible list on 24 August 1989. For more than a decade Rose publicly insisted he had never bet on baseball, before admitting it privately to Commissioner Bud Selig in 2002 and publicly in his autobiography in January 2004. The ban kept him out of the Baseball Hall of Fame.
938.explanation: A compulsive gambler who began betting uncontrollably by 1985 lost his place in the game he loved and then spent years living a public lie about it.
938.tie_back: The kural says gambling ruins wealth and drives a person to lying, and Rose's gambling cost him his career and led him to deny the truth for fifteen years.
938._accuracy_note: Strong fit to gambling producing falsehood and ruin; the kural's further claim about the loss of compassion is not illustrated.

939.event_title: Dostoevsky gambles away his travel money in Wiesbaden and pawns his belongings in Baden-Baden
939.event: In August 1865 Fyodor Dostoevsky gambled away all his travel money at the Wiesbaden casino and was stranded at his hotel for two months, where he was eventually given nothing to eat but tea and the staff stopped serving him, until friends and a Russian Orthodox priest sent money for him to leave. In 1867, having just married Anna Snitkina, he went to Baden-Baden hoping to escape his debts by gambling, and by the end of that summer he had pawned many of his and his wife's belongings and lost the gifts sent by friends to rescue them. He stopped gambling altogether only in 1871.
939.explanation: Even a writer of genius, at work on Crime and Punishment at the time, was reduced by roulette to hunger and pawned possessions.
939.tie_back: The kural says that clothing, wealth, food, renown and learning never reach one who takes up gambling, and Dostoevsky's gambling left him without food in Wiesbaden and without his and his wife's belongings in Baden-Baden.
939._accuracy_note: Hunger and pawned belongings match several of the five goods; his renown and learning were not lost, as he wrote his great novels in the same years.

940.event_title: The Rigveda's Gambler's Lament is composed
940.event: Hymn 10.34 of the Rigveda, more than 3,000 years old, is spoken by a compulsive dice player who says that a losing throw has driven away his devoted wife, that her mother hates him and that his own family disowns him while he wanders in debt. He describes how, whenever he swears he will not play again, the sound of the dice falling sends him running back to the gaming place like a lover to a meeting. The hymn ends with the god Savitr's counsel to stop playing with dice and to till his field and value what he has.
940.explanation: The oldest known poem about gambling addiction already describes the pattern of ruin, resolve and relapse that later gamblers would recognise.
940.tie_back: The kural says gambling is loved all the more the more one loses, and the Rigveda's gambler, having lost wife, family and wealth, still runs back to the dice whenever he hears them.
940._accuracy_note: Almost a dramatisation of the kural's first line; it is a documented ancient text rather than an event in a particular person's life, and translations differ in wording.
